questions.q: You roll two dice and add them. Which sum comes up most often in the long run?

opts.t: 12, because it's the biggest
They're all equally likely: there are 11 sums and each has a 1 in 11 chance
7, because more pairs of dice add up to 7 than to any other sum
2 and 12, because they're at the ends

questions.why: There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely pairs (die 1, die 2). Six of them make 7: 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1. Only one makes 2 (1+1). That's why the columns form a triangle.

questions.q: A password is 3 lowercase letters (repeats allowed). How many are there?

questions.why: Each position is a separate choice of 26 letters, and repeats are allowed, so the multiplication rule gives 26³. perm would forbid repeats like "aaa", and comb would also say "abc" and "cba" are the same password.

questions.q: In your own words: why are the 11 sums of two dice not equally likely, and how would you check a probability like P(sum = 7) without any formula?
questions.a: The equally likely things are the 36 (die 1, die 2) pairs, not the sums. Six pairs make 7 but only one makes 2, so 7 is six times as likely. To check without a formula, simulate: roll two arrays of dice many times with numpy, add them, and take the mean of sums == 7. With enough rolls the frequency settles on the probability (about 0.167).

questions.q: In the "Bread & butter" scenario, 120 customers buy butter and 96 of those also buy bread. What is P(bread | butter)?
questions.why: "Given butter" means we only look at the 120 butter buyers. 96 of them bought bread, so 96/120 = 0.8. Dividing by 400 would answer a different question: P(bread and butter).

questions.q: P(rain) = 0.3 and P(I carry an umbrella) = 0.4. Someone computes P(rain and umbrella) = 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12. What's wrong?

opts.t: Nothing, that's the multiplication rule
They should have added: 0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7
They assumed independence, but I'm much more likely to carry an umbrella when it rains, so the real answer is bigger
Probabilities can't be multiplied

questions.why: The general rule is P(rain and umbrella) = P(rain) × P(umbrella | rain). If P(umbrella | rain) is 0.9, the answer is 0.27, more than twice 0.12. Multiplying the plain probabilities is only allowed when the events are independent.

questions.q: Explain P(A | B) to a friend without a formula, and say how you'd check whether A and B are independent.
questions.a: Throw away everyone who isn't B, then ask what fraction of the people left are A. It's counting inside a smaller world. A and B are independent if that fraction is the same as the fraction of A in the whole crowd: learning B didn't change anything. Equivalently P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). If they're not independent you must use P(A and B) = P(B) × P(A | B).

questions.q: In a town of 1,000, 10 people are sick. The test catches 9 of them, and also flags 89 of the 990 healthy people. Of everyone who tests positive, what fraction is sick?

opts.t: 89 / 990 ≈ 9%, which is a coincidence

questions.why: Everyone who tests positive is 9 + 89 = 98 people, and only 9 of them are sick. The 90% is the share of sick people who test positive, a different question with a different bottom number.

questions.q: Why do spam filters add up logarithms of probabilities instead of multiplying the probabilities?

opts.t: Logarithms make the answer more accurate in principle
Multiplying hundreds of small numbers like 0.001 rounds to 0.0 in floating point; adding logs keeps the information
Python can't multiply more than 100 numbers
Logarithms remove the "naive" assumption

questions.why: log(a × b) = log a + log b, so the comparison is the same, but 0.001²⁰⁰ is 10⁻⁶⁰⁰, far below the smallest float (about 10⁻³⁰⁸). In logs it's just −1381.6, perfectly fine.

questions.q: A test is 99% sensitive and 99% specific, and the condition affects 1 in 10,000 people. Explain, with counts of people, why a positive result still probably means you're healthy.
questions.a: Take 1,000,000 people: 100 are sick and 99 of them test positive. 999,900 are healthy and 1% of them, about 9,999, also test positive. So of roughly 10,098 positives only 99 are sick, under 1%. The base rate is so low that the small false positive rate applied to the huge healthy group swamps the true cases. The fix is a second independent test on the positives: the posterior becomes the new prior.

questions.q: With p = 0.5 and 10 rows, why do so many balls land in the middle bin (5 rights) and so few at the edges (0 or 10 rights)?

opts.t: The pegs in the middle are bigger
Balls bounce toward the centre
Only one route gives 0 rights (left every time), but 252 different routes give exactly 5 rights
It's luck; with more balls it would even out

questions.why: Every single route is equally likely when p = 0.5. The middle bin wins because far more routes end there. Counting those routes is what the binomial formula does.

questions.q: Bus waits are exponential with an average of 10 minutes. You've already waited 10 minutes. How long do you expect to wait now?

opts.t: 0 minutes: it's due
5 minutes
10 more minutes: the exponential has no memory
20 minutes

questions.why: The exponential is memoryless: P(wait > s + t | waited s) = P(wait > t). If buses truly arrive like a Poisson process, the time you've already waited tells you nothing. (Real buses on a timetable aren't like this, which is why the model choice matters.)

questions.q: Explain the binomial formula C(n, k) pᵏ (1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ using the Galton board, and say when you'd use Poisson instead.
questions.a: Each peg is a yes/no trial with chance p of "right". A ball's bin is its number of rights k. Any single route with k rights and n−k lefts has probability pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ because independent chances multiply, and there are C(n, k) such routes, so you multiply the two. Use Poisson when there's no fixed number of trials, just events happening independently at a steady average rate λ in a window of time or space (calls per minute, typos per page).

questions.q: You've rolled a fair die 10 times and the average is 4.6, well above 3.5. What happens to your running average over the next 10,000 rolls?

opts.t: The next rolls will be low, to make up for the high start
It drifts toward 3.5, because 10,000 ordinary rolls swamp the first 10
It stays near 4.6, since you're on a hot streak
It can't be predicted at all

questions.why: Dice have no memory, so nothing "makes up" for the early rolls (believing it does is the gambler's fallacy). The early excess just gets diluted: it's 10 rolls out of 10,010.

questions.q: 100 people throw their hats in a pile and each takes one back at random. On average, how many get their own hat?

opts.t: About 37
Exactly 1

questions.why: Let Xᵢ be 1 if person i gets their own hat. Each has a 1/100 chance, so E[Xᵢ] = 1/100. The total is the sum of 100 of them, and expectations add even though the Xᵢ depend on each other: 100 × 1/100 = 1. (It's 1 for any number of people.)

questions.q: A friend says "the law of large numbers means if I've lost 10 coin flips in a row, I'm due a win". Explain what the law really says, and how fast averages settle.
questions.a: The law says the average of many independent flips gets close to the expected value, not that later flips compensate for earlier ones. Coins have no memory; the next flip is still 50/50. Early streaks get diluted by the many flips that follow, not corrected. And it's slow: the average's typical error is σ/√n, so 100 times more flips only makes the average 10 times more precise.

questions.q: Each sample mean averages n = 25 draws from a source with standard deviation 10. How spread out are the sample means?

opts.t: 10, the same as the source
2, because the spread of an average is σ/√n = 10/5

questions.why: Averages wobble less than single draws, by a factor of √n. With n = 25 that's 5 times less. (Chapter 5 found the same σ/√n from the other direction.)

questions.q: A startup averages the revenue of 10 customers to estimate the typical customer. Revenue is extremely lopsided: most pay 10, a few enterprise customers pay 50,000. Is a normal-based error bar trustworthy?

opts.t: Yes, the CLT always works for n ≥ 10
No: with such a lopsided source, 10 customers is far too few for the average to be near normal; one big customer in or out swings it wildly
Yes, because revenue can't be negative
No, because the CLT only applies to coins and dice

questions.why: The rule of thumb "n ≥ 30" is for mild sources. With one-in-a-hundred giants, the average of 10 is dominated by whether a giant happened to be in the sample. Use the bootstrap (chapter 8) or a median, and look at the data.

questions.q: Explain the central limit theorem to someone who's never heard of it, and say why it makes the bell curve so common.
questions.a: If you add up or average many independent random pieces, the total's distribution looks like a bell, no matter what each piece looked like, as long as no single piece dominates. The bell is centred on the average of the pieces' mean, and its width shrinks like 1/√n for averages. Lots of real quantities (heights, measurement errors, poll results, total sales) are sums of many small independent effects, so they come out bell-shaped. It needs more pieces when each one is very lopsided, and it fails when single pieces can be wildly extreme.

questions.q: A magazine surveys 2.4 million readers (huge!) and predicts the election wrong. A pollster asks 1,500 randomly chosen voters and gets it right. How?

opts.t: 1,500 is the magic number for polls
The magazine's readers weren't like the voters as a whole; a biased sample stays biased however big it is
Big samples have more random error
The pollster got lucky

questions.why: This really happened: the Literary Digest in 1936 polled millions of its (richer-than-average) readers and called the election for the loser. Gallup's much smaller random sample got it right. Size cures random error, not bias.

questions.q: In World War II, analysts mapped bullet holes on bombers returning from missions and proposed adding armour where the holes were densest. Abraham Wald said to armour where there were no holes. Why?

opts.t: Holes were randomly placed, so it didn't matter
Planes hit in the hole-free areas didn't come back; the sample only contained survivors
Armour is heavier in the places with holes
Wald misread the data

questions.why: The returning planes are a survivorship-biased sample. Hits where you never see holes were the deadly ones. A huge sample of returning planes could never reveal that by itself.

questions.q: Your boss says "we got 50,000 responses to our customer survey, so the results must be accurate." What do you say?
questions.a: 50,000 responses make the random error tiny, but they do nothing about bias. Who answered? If the people who chose to respond differ from customers overall (the very happy and the very angry are more likely to bother), the result is precisely wrong. A small random sample, or weighting the responses by known customer groups, would be more trustworthy than a huge self-selected one.

questions.q: You build a 95% interval for average delivery time and get 28 to 35 minutes. Which statement is correct?

opts.t: There is a 95% chance the true average is between 28 and 35
95% of deliveries take between 28 and 35 minutes
The method that produced 28 to 35 catches the true average in about 95% of samples
If you repeat the study, 95% of new averages will land between 28 and 35

questions.why: The true average is a fixed number; it's either in [28, 35] or not. The 95% describes how often the procedure works. (The second option mixes up the average with single deliveries, which vary much more.)

Nothing changes; confidence only affects the wording
The average moves closer to the truth

questions.q: Explain to a friend what "a 95% confidence interval of 28 to 35 minutes" means, why the interval narrows as n grows, and why small samples use t instead of 1.96.
questions.a: The procedure that made [28, 35] catches the true average in about 95 of 100 samples; this particular interval either caught it or didn't. Its width is about 2 × multiplier × s/√n, so it shrinks like 1/√n (4x the data halves it). With small n the sample sd s is itself unreliable and often too small, so 1.96 would under-cover (about 88% at n = 5); the t multiplier is larger for small n to make the promise true. When no formula exists (median, percentiles), resample the data with replacement (the bootstrap) and take the middle 95% of the recomputed statistic.

questions.q: After 1,000 shuffles, 21 of the shuffled gaps were at least as big as the real one. What does that tell you?

opts.t: There's a 2.1% chance the new page works
There's a 97.9% chance the new page works
If the page made no difference, luck alone would produce a gap this big about 2.1% of the time
The new page adds 2.1% more sign-ups

questions.why: That's the definition of a p-value: the probability of data at least this extreme assuming the null hypothesis is true. It isn't the probability that the null (or the alternative) is true. That needs a prior: chapter 11.

opts.t: Yes: p < 0.05 means the effect is large
Not much: the effect is real but tiny; whether 0.02 points matters is a business question, not a p-value question
No: p = 0.003 means the result is probably a fluke
No: a p-value can't be computed with 2 million users

questions.why: With huge samples, even microscopic effects become "significant". Significance says the effect probably isn't zero; it says nothing about whether it's big enough to care about.

questions.q: Explain a p-value to a friend who runs a bakery and tried a new recipe on some days, without using the words "null hypothesis".
questions.a: Suppose the recipe made no difference at all. Then which days happened to get the new recipe is just luck of the draw. If I reshuffle which days count as "new recipe" thousands of times, I see how big a difference luck alone tends to make. The p-value is how often luck matched or beat the difference you actually saw. A small p-value means luck rarely does that, so the recipe probably did something. It doesn't say how much, or guarantee it, and if you try twenty recipes some will look good by luck.

questions.q: Why does one far-away outlier move the least-squares line so much?

opts.t: Outliers have more weight in the formula by design
Its miss gets squared, so a miss 5 times bigger counts 25 times as much, and the line tilts to reduce it
The line has to pass through every point
It doesn't; least squares ignores outliers

questions.why: Squaring is what makes the maths neat (one exact best line), and also what makes it sensitive: a single big residual can dominate the total. Always plot your data before trusting a fitted line.

questions.q: A study finds that people who drink more coffee live longer. What's the most careful conclusion?

opts.t: Coffee makes you live longer
Living longer makes you drink coffee
Coffee drinking and longevity are associated; something else (income, health, habits) could drive both, so this alone doesn't show coffee causes it
The study must be wrong

questions.why: Observational data shows association. Healthier, wealthier people might both drink more coffee and live longer. Only a randomised experiment (or strong causal reasoning) separates cause from confounding.

questions.q: Explain what "least squares" means and name two ways a regression line can mislead you.
questions.a: Among all straight lines, least squares picks the one with the smallest total of squared vertical misses: each point's error is squared and the squares are added. It can mislead when (1) an outlier, because squaring makes big misses dominate and drags the line toward one strange point, and (2) when you read the slope as cause and effect: a confounder can make two things move together without one causing the other. It also only captures straight-line patterns, so always plot the data and the residuals.

questions.q: Bo started out very sure the coin favoured tails. Why did his belief still end up near Ada's?

opts.t: Bayes' rule ignores the prior
Each flip multiplies in more evidence; after many flips the likelihood is so sharp that it outweighs any reasonable prior
Bo changed his mind on purpose
The coin changed its bias

questions.why: The prior counts like a fixed number of imaginary flips. Real flips keep piling up, so eventually they dominate. Only a prior that says "impossible" (a bar at exactly zero) can never be overturned, which is why careful Bayesians avoid zeros.

questions.q: After 7 heads in 10 flips with a flat prior, the 90% credible interval for p is about (0.45, 0.86). Which statement is correct?

opts.t: Given the flat prior and these flips, there's a 90% probability that p is between 0.45 and 0.86
90% of future flips will be between 0.45 and 0.86
p is 0.7 for sure; the interval is just rounding
If you repeated the experiment, 90% of the time you'd get 7 heads

questions.why: A credible interval is a direct probability statement about the unknown, conditional on the prior. That's its big advantage, and its cost: someone with a different prior would report a different interval.

questions.q: Explain how Bayesian inference updates a belief about an unknown number, and why two people with different priors end up agreeing.
questions.a: Write down a belief about the unknown as a distribution over its possible values (the prior). For each value, compute how likely the observed data would be (the likelihood). Multiply prior by likelihood and rescale to get the posterior: values that explain the data well gain belief. With few data points the prior matters a lot; but each new observation multiplies in more evidence, the likelihood gets sharper, and it eventually swamps any prior that doesn't rule the truth out completely, so people with different reasonable priors converge.

questions.q: With step size 1 the walker stayed on the left island. Why?

opts.t: The right island has less probability
Every small step into the valley is a big drop in height, so it's nearly always refused; small steps can't reach the other island
The walker is programmed to stay where it started
Step size 1 means it never moves

questions.why: The chain is still correct in theory, it would get there eventually, but "eventually" could be millions of steps. Real samplers fail like this all the time, which is why people run several chains from different starting points and check they agree.

questions.code:
P = np.array([[0.9, 0.1],     # sunny -> sunny, rainy
              [0.5, 0.5]])    # rainy -> sunny, rainy
d = np.array([0.0, 1.0])      # it's raining today
for day in range(1, 4):
    d = d @ P
    print(day, d.round(3))

questions.title: One Metropolis step
questions.tests:
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
logp = lambda x: -0.5 * x * x
xs = [0.0]
for _ in range(4000):
    xs.append(metropolis_step(xs[-1], logp, 1.0, rng))
assert abs(np.mean(xs)) < 0.2 and 0.8 < np.std(xs) < 1.2, "samples a standard normal"

questions.q: A sampler accepts 99% of its proposals. What's the likely problem?

opts.t: Nothing, a high acceptance rate is ideal
The steps are tiny, so it barely moves and explores very slowly
The steps are huge
The target distribution is wrong

questions.why: Tiny steps are almost always accepted because the height barely changes, but the walker crawls. Huge steps are mostly rejected. A common rule of thumb for one-dimensional targets is to aim for roughly 40–50% acceptance, and lower in many dimensions.

questions.q: Explain what a stationary distribution is and how the Metropolis rule uses it to draw samples from a shape you can't sample directly.
questions.a: A Markov chain hops between states using only the current state. Many chains settle into a long-run pattern where the fraction of time in each state stops changing: that's the stationary distribution, π @ P = π. Metropolis designs a chain whose stationary distribution is the target: propose a nearby point, always accept if it's higher, accept with probability new/old if it's lower. Only ratios of heights are needed, so unknown normalising constants cancel. Run it long enough and the time spent in each region matches the target; but if steps are too small or too big it explores slowly, so you check acceptance rates and run several chains.

questions.q: In the A/A test the two pages are identical, yet peeking after every 100 visitors declared a winner about a quarter of the time. Why?

opts.t: The random number generator is biased
The z-score wobbles as data arrives; each look is another chance for it to wander past 1.96 by luck, and stopping at the first crossing keeps that lucky moment
5% is only an approximation
Identical pages can't be tested

questions.why: "p < 0.05" promises a 5% false-alarm rate for one look decided in advance. Twenty looks with "stop when it's significant" gives about 25%. Fix the sample size before you start, or use a method designed for repeated looks.

questions.code:
cA, nA, cB, nB = 100, 1000, 120, 1000
p = (cA + cB) / (nA + nB)
se = math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) * (1 / nA + 1 / nB))
z = (cB / nB - cA / nA) / se
print(round(z, 3), round(math.erfc(abs(z) / math.sqrt(2)), 4))

questions.q: The same data gives p = 0.15 and "P(B better) = 92%". Which is a fair summary for a manager?

opts.t: The test failed, so B is no better
B is 92% better than A
B is probably better, but the evidence is weak: with a flat prior, about a 1-in-12 chance A is actually better, and the lift could be tiny
The two numbers contradict each other, so the test is broken

questions.why: They answer different questions. The p-value says a gap this size would turn up 15% of the time by chance alone. The Bayesian number says how plausible "B is better" is, given the data and a flat prior. Neither says how much better: report an interval for the lift too.

questions.q: Explain how to run an A/B test honestly: what you decide before starting, how you analyse it, and the two classic ways people fool themselves.
questions.a: Before starting, choose one metric, the smallest lift worth acting on, the false-alarm rate (usually 5%) and the power (usually 80%), and from those compute the sample size; write down the stopping rule. Run until that size, then do one two-proportion test: z is the gap in rates divided by its standard error, giving a p-value, and report the lift with a confidence interval (and, if useful, the Bayesian probability B is better). The classic traps: peeking (checking repeatedly and stopping at the first significant result inflates false alarms far above 5%) and multiple comparisons (testing many variants or metrics and reporting the winner); fix the second with a correction like Bonferroni, dividing alpha by the number of tests.
